In brief

As Gerty exposes her underwear, she sees the stranger on the beach "literally worshipping at her shrine." The choice of adverbs is comically inept: the only thing Bloom is doing literally is masturbating. Joyce repeats here a verbal trick that he had played once before in "The Dead," but this time the literal and metaphorical meanings come much closer to coinciding, thanks to the Marian imagery he carried over from one passage to the other.

At more length

The final story of Dubliners opens with this sentence: "Lily, the caretaker's daughter, was literally run off her feet." The next sentence does not describe a nasty fall to the floor, but only a whirlwind of hectic labor: "Hardly had she brought one gentleman into the little pantry behind the office on the ground floor and helped him off with his overcoat than the wheezy hall-door bell clanged again and she had to scamper along the bare hallway to let in another guest." The misused adverb is a notable example of Joyce's cherished device of free indirect style: Lily is a poor uneducated servant girl who would use words in this way if she were telling the story. Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner cite evidence in the OED that "The use of the word literally as an intensifier—and thus in a sense that can be directly opposite to its literal meaning—dates back to the mid-eighteenth century and became increasingly common in the nineteenth century."

Marian echoes swirl around the names of Lily and of the protagonist of the story. Gabriel is the archangel who comes to tell Mary that she will give birth to the son of God, and Mary is often associated with white lilies because of her sexual purity (numerous Renaissance paintings of the Annunciation place such a lily in the scene). As often happens in "The Dead," the symbolic resonances of these two names prove elusive, subject to ambiguous interpretation. In Nausicaa, however, the implication is unmistakable: sexual adoration resembles religious adoration. What Bloom is doing in response to the blue-clad virgin on the beach is not all that different from what the men in the nearby church are doing in response to their blue-clad Virgin. 

Craving a vagina may not be precisely the same thing as entreating the help of the Mother of God, but the parallel insinuates a symbolic equivalence. Gerty is not entirely wrong to suppose that Bloom is literally worshiping her.

John Hunt 2026
